States of Matter and Mixtures
Everything you touch is matter

Air, water, steel, your phone screen, your own body. All of it is matter : anything that has mass and takes up space. Chemistry starts with one simple question: what is this stuff made of, and how does it behave? In this lesson you will learn the states matter can be in, how mixtures differ from pure substances, and how we pull mixtures apart. These ideas explain why tea dissolves sugar, why salt is made from sea water, and why petrol is separated from crude oil.
Particles in constant motion

All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms and molecules). The states of matter differ in how these particles are arranged and how freely they move. Solid: particles locked in place, only vibrating. Fixed shape and volume. Liquid: particles close but sliding past each other. Fixed volume, takes the shape of its container. Gas: particles far apart and zooming around. No fixed shape or volume. Think of a packed train compartment (solid), a busy railway platform (liquid) and an open ground full of running children (gas).
Changing state: heat moves particles

Adding heat makes particles move faster. At the melting point a solid becomes liquid. At the boiling point a liquid becomes gas. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. Other changes have names: sublimation (solid straight to gas, like camphor or dry ice) and condensation (gas to liquid). During melting or boiling the temperature stays flat, because the heat is used to loosen particles, not to speed them up.
The fourth state: plasma

Heat a gas enough and atoms lose electrons. You get a soup of charged particles called plasma . It is the most common state in the universe: the Sun and all stars are plasma. On Earth you see it in lightning, neon signs and the glow of a tube light. Temperature scales matter too. Scientists use kelvin: K = °C + 273 . So 25 °C is 298 K. Zero kelvin (about -273 °C) is the coldest possible temperature.
Pure substances and mixtures

A pure substance has fixed composition. It is either an element (one kind of atom, like iron) or a compound (different atoms bonded in a fixed ratio, like water, H2O). A mixture is two or more substances jumbled together, not chemically bonded, in any proportion. Homogeneous: looks uniform (salt water, air, brass). Also called a solution. Heterogeneous: you can see the parts (sand in water, salad, granite). Key test: a compound can only be split by a chemical reaction. A mixture can be split by physical means.
How we separate mixtures

Each method uses a difference in physical property. Filtration: solid from liquid (size). Evaporation: dissolved solid from liquid (boiling point). Distillation: liquids with different boiling points. Crude oil is split this way into petrol, diesel and kerosene. Magnet: iron filings from sand. Chromatography: ink spots travel at different speeds on paper. Centrifuge: cream from milk, or blood cells from plasma, by spinning.
Density and concentration

Density = mass / volume. A metal block has mass 54 g and volume 20 cm3. Density = 54 / 20 = 2.7 g/cm3 . That matches aluminium, so the block is probably aluminium. Water is 1 g/cm3, so things below this float. Mass percent = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100. Dissolve 5 g salt in 95 g water. Solution mass = 100 g. Concentration = 5 / 100 x 100 = 5 percent .
Common mix-ups

Water is not a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen. It is a compound with new properties; you cannot separate it by filtering. Steam is invisible. The white cloud above a kettle is tiny liquid droplets, not gas. Dissolving is not melting. Sugar in tea is a mixture; the sugar is still sugar. Air is not one gas. It is a mixture: about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, rest argon, CO2 and others.
Salt from the sea

India is among the world's top salt producers. In Gujarat (Kutch, Mithapur) and Tamil Nadu, sea water or brine is let into shallow pans. Sun and wind evaporate the water and salt crystals remain. It is the oldest chemical separation, and it is just evaporation and crystallisation. Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan, India's largest inland salt lake, is worked the same way. Salt, a compound of sodium and chlorine, is separated from a mixture using nothing but sunlight.
Key takeaways

Solid, liquid, gas and plasma differ in particle freedom. Pure substances are elements or compounds; mixtures can be split physically. Separation methods exploit differences in size, boiling point, magnetism or speed. Density = mass/volume; K = °C + 273. Think about it 1. Why does the temperature stay at 100 °C while water boils, even though the stove keeps heating? 2. How would you separate a mixture of sand, salt and iron filings?
Atoms, Isotopes and the Mole
Counting the uncountable

A single drop of water holds more than a billion billion molecules. Chemists cannot count atoms one by one, so they invented a counting unit, the mole . It is the bridge between the invisible world of atoms and the grams you weigh on a lab balance. First, though, we need to know what an atom is.
The atom and its parts

An atom has a tiny dense nucleus with protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral), and electrons (negative) around it. The atom is mostly empty space: if the nucleus were a marble, the atom would be a stadium. Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. It defines the element. Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons. Example: sodium, Z = 11, A = 23, so it has 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons.
How we found the parts

John Dalton, 1808: atoms are the basic building blocks; each element has its own kind. J.J. Thomson, 1897: discovered the electron. Ernest Rutherford, 1911: gold-foil experiment showed a small dense nucleus (proton named about 1919). James Chadwick, 1932: discovered the neutron.
Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Same protons, so same chemistry, but different mass. Hydrogen: protium (0 neutrons), deuterium (1), tritium (2). Carbon-12 and carbon-14. Carbon-14 is radioactive and used in dating old remains. Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. This is why the periodic table shows chlorine as 35.5: it is a weighted average. Chlorine is about 75 percent Cl-35 and 25 percent Cl-37. Average = 0.75 x 35 + 0.25 x 37 = 35.5 .
Atomic mass and the mole

One carbon-12 atom is defined as exactly 12 atomic mass units. We weigh atoms relative to it. The mole is a count: 6.022 x 10^23 particles, called the Avogadro constant (named after Amedeo Avogadro, whose 1811 idea about gases inspired it). A mole of carbon-12 weighs exactly 12 g. So the molar mass in g/mol equals the atomic or molecular mass in units. Dozen = 12 things; mole = 6.022 x 10^23 things.
Mole formulas

Three relations cover most problems. Formulas moles = mass (g) / molar mass (g/mol) number of particles = moles x 6.022 x 10^23 molar mass of a compound = sum of atomic masses Water: H2O = 2 x 1 + 16 = 18 g/mol . CO2 = 12 + 2 x 16 = 44 g/mol . NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol.
From grams to molecules

How many moles and molecules are in 36 g of water? Molar mass of water = 18 g/mol. Moles = 36 / 18 = 2 mol . Molecules = 2 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 1.2 x 10^24 . Another: how many grams in 0.5 mol of NaCl? Mass = 0.5 x 58.5 = 29.25 g .
Where students slip

A mole is not a mass. It is a number. A mole of feathers and a mole of lead have the same count, different masses. Isotopes are not different elements. They differ only in neutrons. Atoms are not solid balls. They are mostly empty space. Mass number is not atomic mass exactly. Mass number is a whole count; atomic mass is a measured average.
Kanada and heavy water

Long before Dalton, the Vaisheshika school in ancient India, associated with the philosopher Kanada , argued that matter is made of indivisible particles called paramanu . It was philosophy, not experiment, but it shows early atomic thinking. In modern times, India runs heavy-water plants under the Department of Atomic Energy. Heavy water contains deuterium, the hydrogen isotope with one neutron, and is used as a moderator in India's pressurised heavy-water reactors.
Key takeaways

Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes share protons but differ in neutrons. 1 mole = 6.022 x 10^23 particles; molar mass links grams to moles. moles = mass / molar mass. Think about it 1. Why do isotopes of one element behave almost identically in chemical reactions? 2. Which has more atoms: 12 g of carbon or 12 g of magnesium (24 g/mol)?
Atomic Structure and Orbitals
Why elements have personalities

Sodium explodes in water; neon does nothing. Both are made of protons, neutrons and electrons. The difference lies in how electrons are arranged. Electron arrangement decides almost all of chemistry: colour, bonding, reactivity, even why lasers work.
Bohr's shells

Niels Bohr, 1913 , proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus only in fixed energy levels (shells). An electron can jump up by absorbing exact energy, and falls down by releasing it as light. That explained why hydrogen glows in specific colours only: each colour is one jump. Shells hold at most 2n^2 electrons: 2, 8, 18 for n = 1, 2, 3.
The quantum picture

Bohr's orbits were too simple. In the 1920s, de Broglie (1924) said electrons behave like waves, Schrödinger (1926) wrote the wave equation, and Heisenberg (1927) showed we cannot know both position and speed exactly. So we speak of orbitals : regions where an electron is most likely found, not tracks.
Orbitals: s, p, d, f

s: spherical. 1 orbital, holds 2 electrons. p: dumbbell. 3 orbitals, holds 6. d: clover. 5 orbitals, holds 10. f: complex. 7 orbitals, holds 14. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons with opposite spin. Shell 1 has only 1s; shell 2 has 2s and 2p; shell 3 has 3s, 3p, 3d.
Filling rules

Aufbau: fill the lowest energy first: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p. Pauli exclusion (1925): no two electrons share all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds max 2. Hund's rule: in a set of equal orbitals, spread electrons singly first, like passengers taking empty bus seats before doubling up.
Writing configurations

Count electrons, fill in order. Hydrogen (1): 1s1 Carbon (6): 1s2 2s2 2p2 Sodium (11): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 Neon (10): 1s2 2s2 2p6, a full outer shell Sodium has one lonely outer electron, easily lost. Neon's outer shell is full, so it is content and inert. That is the whole story of their different behaviour.
Configuration of chlorine

Chlorine has 17 electrons. 1s2 uses 2 (15 left). 2s2 2p6 uses 8 (7 left). 3s2 3p5 uses 7 (0 left). Configuration: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5 . Outer shell has 7 electrons, one short of full, so chlorine grabs an electron to become Cl-. It also becomes isoelectronic with argon (18 electrons).
Clearing up

Electrons do not orbit like planets. Orbitals are probability clouds. An orbital is not the same as an orbit. 4s fills before 3d , because it is slightly lower in energy for neutral atoms. Light from atoms is not random. Each colour corresponds to a precise energy jump.
Bose and Raman

Satyendra Nath Bose (1924) developed the statistics of light particles, later extended by Einstein into Bose-Einstein statistics. The particle class boson carries his name. C.V. Raman discovered in 1928 that light scattered by molecules changes colour slightly, revealing molecular energy levels. The Raman effect won him the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, and Raman spectroscopy is now a standard chemistry tool.
Key takeaways

Electrons occupy quantised energy levels and orbitals (s, p, d, f). Shell capacity is 2n^2; s, p, d, f hold 2, 6, 10, 14. Fill by Aufbau, Pauli and Hund. Outer electrons decide chemical behaviour. Think about it 1. Why does neon not react while sodium does? 2. Write the configuration of magnesium (12 electrons).
The Periodic Table and Its Trends
A map of all matter

The periodic table is chemistry's most useful chart. With one glance you can guess how an element behaves, what it bonds with and what it looks like. It even let scientists predict elements before they were found.
Mendeleev's insight

Dmitri Mendeleev, 1869 , arranged the known elements by increasing atomic mass and noticed that properties repeat at regular intervals. He left gaps for unknown elements and predicted their properties. He predicted eka-aluminium . In 1875 Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium , matching the prediction closely. That success made the table famous.
Moseley fixes the order

Henry Moseley, 1913 , used X-rays to show that the real ordering principle is atomic number (protons), not mass. The modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number. This fixed oddities like tellurium and iodine, where mass order disagreed with properties.
Reading the layout

Periods: 7 horizontal rows. Same number of shells. Groups: 18 vertical columns. Same outer electrons, similar chemistry. Blocks: s, p, d, f, named after the orbital being filled. Famous groups: Group 1 alkali metals (Li, Na, K), Group 2 alkaline earths, Group 17 halogens, Group 18 noble gases. Metals sit left and centre, non-metals right, with metalloids (like silicon) on the staircase between.
Trend 1: atomic size
Atomic radius decreases across a period (left to right): more protons pull the same shell tighter. It increases down a group : extra shells are added. So caesium is huge, fluorine is tiny.
Trends 2 and 3: ionisation energy, electronegativity

Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove an electron. It rises across a period and falls down a group. That is why Group 1 metals lose electrons so easily. Electronegativity (Linus Pauling's scale) is the pull on shared electrons. It rises towards the top right. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0). Reactivity follows: metals get more reactive going down a group (K is more reactive than Na); non-metals get more reactive going up (F more than I).
Predict from position

Element X is in Period 3, Group 17. Which element? Chlorine. It has 7 outer electrons, so it is a reactive non-metal that forms X- ions and bonds with Group 1 metals like sodium to make NaCl. Compare size: Na (Period 3, Group 1) vs Cl (Period 3, Group 17). Across the period size shrinks, so Na is larger than Cl. Compare Li and K: same group, K is lower, so K is larger and loses its electron more easily.
Be careful

Hydrogen is not an alkali metal , though placed in Group 1. Mendeleev did not know protons. Atomic number came later. Larger atoms are not harder to ionise. The outer electron is farther away and easier to remove. There are 118 known elements , the last (oganesson) completing Period 7.
Saha and monazite sands

Meghnad Saha derived the Saha ionisation equation in 1920, explaining how atoms of different elements ionise at different star temperatures. It is the basis for reading the chemistry of stars. India's coastal sands in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha are rich in monazite , a mineral holding rare-earth elements and thorium, which links the periodic table directly to India's nuclear plans.
Key takeaways

Mendeleev (1869) arranged by mass; Moseley (1913) showed atomic number is the true order. 18 groups, 7 periods; groups share outer-electron count. Radius falls across, rises down; ionisation energy and electronegativity rise across. Think about it 1. Why is potassium more reactive than lithium? 2. Why did Mendeleev's gaps make his table convincing?
Ionic and Covalent Bonds
Why atoms stick together

Table salt, water, diamond, iron: each holds together in a different way. Atoms bond because the bonded arrangement has lower energy than separate atoms. Most atoms bond to reach a full outer shell, the octet rule (eight outer electrons; two for hydrogen and helium).
Three ways to settle the electron bill

Ionic: one atom hands electrons to another. Covalent: atoms share electrons. Metallic: atoms pool electrons in a shared sea. Which one happens depends on electronegativity, the pull each atom has on electrons. A big difference gives ionic, a small one gives covalent.
Ionic bonds

Sodium has one outer electron, chlorine needs one. Sodium gives it away: Na → Na+ + e-, and Cl + e- → Cl- The opposite charges attract strongly: NaCl . Ions pack into a 3D crystal lattice , not separate molecules. Metals and non-metals typically make ionic compounds (e.g. MgO, CaCl2).
Properties of ionic compounds

High melting and boiling points (strong lattice). NaCl melts at about 801 °C. Hard but brittle: shifting a layer lines up like charges, which repel and crack. Do not conduct as solids; conduct when molten or dissolved, because ions can move. Often soluble in water.
Covalent bonds

G.N. Lewis, 1916 , proposed that atoms share electron pairs. Two hydrogens share a pair to form H2. Oxygen shares two pairs with another oxygen: a double bond (O=O). Nitrogen N2 has a triple bond , which is why it is so unreactive. Water: oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen. Written H-O-H. Non-metals bond covalently with each other.
Polar bonds and metallic bonds

In H-Cl, chlorine pulls electrons harder, so the bond is polar : slight negative on Cl, slight positive on H. Equal sharing (H2, Cl2) is non-polar. In metals, outer electrons are free and form a sea of electrons around positive ions. That explains shine, conduction of electricity and heat, and bendability (malleable and ductile). Covalent compounds like sugar or wax usually have low melting points and do not conduct. Giant covalent solids, like diamond, are the exception: extremely hard with very high melting points.
Predict the formula

Magnesium (2 outer electrons) and chlorine (needs 1). Mg gives 2 electrons, so each Cl takes 1: need two Cl. Formula: MgCl2 , made of Mg2+ and 2 Cl-. Charges balance: +2 - 2 = 0. Calcium with oxygen: Ca2+ and O2-: CaO (quicklime). Aluminium Al3+ with oxygen O2-: swap charges to get Al2O3 . Covalent: carbon needs 4, hydrogen 1, so CH4. Nitrogen needs 3: NH3.
Watch out

NaCl is not a molecule. It is a lattice, so we call it a formula unit. Ionic and covalent are not strict boxes. Bonds fall on a scale from fully ionic to fully covalent. Covalent does not mean weak. Diamond is covalent and the hardest natural material. Only the forces between separate molecules are weak.
P.C. Ray and Bengal Chemicals

Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861-1944) made mercurous nitrite in 1896, a stable compound that brought him international recognition. He founded Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works in 1901, among India's first modern chemical companies, and wrote A History of Hindu Chemistry . He showed Indian chemistry could be both research and enterprise.
Key takeaways

Ionic: electron transfer, lattice, high melting point, conducts when molten. Covalent: shared pairs; single, double, triple bonds. Metallic: sea of electrons. Electronegativity difference guides the bond type. Think about it 1. Why does solid salt not conduct electricity but salt water does? 2. Why is nitrogen gas so unreactive?
Molecular Shapes and Intermolecular Forces
Shape is destiny

Water is a liquid but CO2 is a gas, though both are small molecules. Ice floats. A key fits one lock. Enzymes bind only the right molecule. All of this comes from molecular shape and the weak forces between molecules.
VSEPR: electron pairs repel

VSEPR (valence shell electron pair repulsion) says that electron pairs around a central atom spread as far apart as possible, like balloons tied together. The shape follows from counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Common shapes

CO2: linear, 180°. Two bonding groups. BF3: flat triangle, 120°. CH4: tetrahedral, about 109.5°. Four bonds. NH3: pyramidal, about 107°. Three bonds plus one lone pair. H2O: bent, about 104.5°. Two bonds plus two lone pairs. Lone pairs push harder than bonding pairs, squeezing the angles smaller.
Polar molecules

A molecule is polar if its bond polarities do not cancel. CO2 has two polar C=O bonds, but they point opposite ways and cancel: non-polar . Water is bent, so its polarities add: polar . Rule of thumb: like dissolves like. Polar solvents (water) dissolve polar or ionic substances; non-polar solvents (petrol) dissolve oils.
Forces between molecules

These are far weaker than bonds but control boiling point and state. London dispersion forces: brief electron shifts create tiny dipoles. Present in all molecules, stronger with size. Explains why bigger alkanes are liquids. Dipole-dipole: positive end of one polar molecule attracts negative end of another. Hydrogen bond: a special strong dipole attraction when H is attached to N, O or F, and meets a lone pair on another N, O or F.
Why water is strange

Hydrogen bonds give water a high boiling point (100 °C) compared with H2S (about -60 °C). Water is also densest at about 4 °C; as it freezes, hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open lattice, so ice is less dense and floats . Lakes freeze from the top, letting fish survive below. Hydrogen bonds also hold the two strands of DNA together and give proteins their folded shapes.
Predict shape and boiling order

Shape of PH3: phosphorus has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair, like NH3. So pyramidal . Shape of CCl4: four bonds, no lone pairs: tetrahedral , and non-polar since the bonds cancel. Boiling order of CH4, H2O, HCl: CH4 (only weak dispersion, -162 °C) lowest; HCl (dipole-dipole, -85 °C) middle; H2O (hydrogen bonds, 100 °C) highest.
Careful

Hydrogen bonds are not true bonds ; they are attractions between molecules, about a tenth as strong as covalent bonds. Boiling does not break covalent bonds. Boiling water leaves H2O molecules intact, only separated. Having polar bonds does not make a molecule polar ; shape matters.
Ramachandran and protein folding

G.N. Ramachandran (Madras, 1963) worked out which twist angles are allowed in protein chains, drawn as the Ramachandran plot , still used worldwide. He also helped decipher the triple-helix structure of collagen. His work shows that shape and hydrogen bonding decide how a protein folds.
Key takeaways

VSEPR: electron pairs spread out; lone pairs squeeze angles. CH4 109.5, NH3 107, H2O 104.5, CO2 180. Polarity depends on shape. Dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonds set boiling points; hydrogen bonds make ice float. Think about it 1. Why is CO2 non-polar although C=O bonds are polar? 2. If ice sank, what would happen to ponds in winter?
Chemical Equations and Stoichiometry
A recipe for atoms

A cook knows that two eggs and a cup of flour give a certain number of pancakes. Chemists do the same with atoms. Stoichiometry is the arithmetic of reactions: how much of each ingredient you need, and how much product you get. It runs fertiliser plants, medicine factories and your car's engine.
Atoms are never lost

Antoine Lavoisier, 1789 , showed that in a closed system mass is conserved. Atoms rearrange; none are created or destroyed. So every chemical equation must be balanced : same number of each atom on both sides. Also, Joseph Proust (1799) found that a compound always has the same mass ratio of elements. Water is always 1 part hydrogen to 8 parts oxygen by mass.
Balancing an equation

Hydrogen burns in oxygen. Unbalanced: H2 + O2 → H2O (2 O on the left, 1 on the right). Put 2 in front of H2O: H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Now O is balanced. H is now 4 on right, so put 2 before H2. 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Never change small subscripts (that changes the substance); only change the big coefficients in front.
Coefficients are mole ratios

The numbers in 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O mean 2 mol H2 react with 1 mol O2 to give 2 mol H2O. In grams: 4 g H2 + 32 g O2 → 36 g water. Mass in = mass out (4 + 32 = 36). Another: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 (ammonia). 1 mol nitrogen needs 3 mol hydrogen, giving 2 mol ammonia.
The stoichiometry steps
Almost every problem follows the same path.
Limiting reagent and yield

If you have 10 bread slices and 3 cheese slices, you can make only 3 sandwiches. Cheese is the limiting reagent : it runs out first and caps the product. The other is in excess. Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100. Real reactions seldom give 100 percent, because of side reactions and losses.
How much water from 4 g hydrogen?

Moles of H2 = 4 / 2 = 2 mol. 2H2 → 2H2O is a 1:1 ratio, so 2 mol H2O. Mass = 2 x 18 = 36 g . Limiting reagent test: 4 g H2 with 16 g O2. Moles H2 = 2; moles O2 = 0.5. H2 needs half as much O2: 2 mol H2 needs 1 mol O2. We have only 0.5, so O2 is limiting. Water made = 2 x 0.5 = 1 mol = 18 g.
Common errors

Do not balance by changing subscripts. H2O2 is not H2O. Coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios. The limiting reagent is not the one with less mass but the one that runs out first in mole terms. Mass is conserved, moles are not always. 3 mol reactants can become 2 mol product.
Fertiliser factories

Ammonia from N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 (the Haber-Bosch process) is the base of urea fertiliser. India's first large fertiliser plant at Sindri (now in Jharkhand) began producing in 1951, backing the push for food security. Plants calculate stoichiometry daily: how much natural gas, air and steam give each tonne of urea. India is among the world's largest fertiliser consumers.
Key takeaways

Balance equations by coefficients so atoms match. Coefficients give mole ratios; convert grams to moles and back. Limiting reagent controls the product; percent yield compares real to theoretical. Think about it 1. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO: how many grams of MgO from 24 g Mg (24 g/mol)? 2. Why do factories sometimes add one reactant in deliberate excess?
Energy in Reactions: Thermochemistry
Why fuels burn and ice packs chill

Every reaction either releases or absorbs energy. Burning LPG warms your kitchen; an instant cold pack chills a sprain. Thermochemistry measures these energy changes, which decide whether a fuel is useful and whether a reaction will happen on its own.
Exothermic and endothermic

Chemical bonds store energy. Breaking bonds costs energy; forming bonds releases it. Exothermic: more energy released than absorbed. Surroundings get hotter. Burning, rusting, neutralisation. Endothermic: net energy absorbed. Surroundings get colder. Photosynthesis, melting ice, dissolving ammonium nitrate in an ice pack.
Enthalpy change

Enthalpy change (delta H) is the heat exchanged at constant pressure, in kJ per mole. Exothermic reactions have negative delta H, endothermic positive. Methane burning: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, delta H is about -890 kJ/mol . One mole of methane (16 g) releases 890 kJ.
Measuring heat: calorimetry

Heat absorbed by water: q = m x c x delta T , where c is specific heat. For water, c = 4.18 J per gram per °C. This explains why coastal cities have mild climates: water needs a lot of heat to warm up, so it stores and releases heat slowly.
Hess's law

Germain Hess, 1840 : the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or several. Heat is a state function: it depends only on start and end, not the route. This lets us calculate energies we cannot measure directly. Add the delta H values of steps, like adding the height gained over each flight of stairs. Also, delta H of reaction can be estimated as (bonds broken) minus (bonds formed), using bond energies.
Will it happen? Entropy and Gibbs energy

Being exothermic is not enough. Entropy (S) measures disorder: more ways to arrange energy and particles. Nature favours more disorder (second law of thermodynamics). Gibbs energy: delta G = delta H - T delta S. A reaction is spontaneous if delta G is negative. Ice melts above 0 °C even though melting is endothermic, because the entropy gain wins at higher T. Spontaneous does not mean fast; diamond turning to graphite is spontaneous but takes forever.
Heat to warm water

How much heat warms 100 g of water from 25 °C to 45 °C? q = m c delta T = 100 x 4.18 x 20 = 8,360 J (8.36 kJ). How much heat from burning 2 mol methane (delta H = -890 kJ/mol)? 2 x 890 = 1,780 kJ released. In grams: 2 mol x 16 g/mol = 32 g of methane.
Not quite

Heat and temperature are different. A bathtub of warm water holds more heat than a cup of boiling water. Exothermic does not mean explosive. Rusting is exothermic but very slow. Negative delta H means energy leaves the system , it is not 'less energy' in a bad sense. Breaking bonds absorbs energy ; it does not release it.
Cooking fuels and biogas

Most Indian homes cook with LPG (propane and butane), which releases large heat per kilogram. The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (2016) gave millions of rural households LPG connections, replacing smoky wood and dung and cutting indoor air pollution. Rural biogas plants convert cattle dung to methane, whose burning is the exothermic reaction above.
Key takeaways

Exothermic: delta H negative; endothermic: positive. q = m c delta T; Hess's law adds step energies. Spontaneity: delta G = delta H - T delta S, negative means spontaneous. Think about it 1. Why does sweating cool the body (evaporation is endothermic)? 2. Can an endothermic reaction be spontaneous? How?
Rates of Reaction
Fast, slow and never

Petrol burns in a flash; iron rusts over years; diamonds last forever, even though graphite is more stable. Chemical kinetics studies how fast reactions go and why. Controlling speed is the heart of cooking, medicine shelf-life and industrial profit.
Collision theory

For particles to react they must collide , with enough energy and in the right orientation. Most collisions fail, like trying to snap a stick with a gentle tap. The minimum energy needed is the activation energy . Svante Arrhenius (1889) showed how rate depends on it: lower activation energy or higher temperature means a faster reaction.
The energy hill
Imagine pushing a boulder over a hill before it rolls down. The hill is the activation energy. Even an exothermic reaction needs this push. A match gives the initial energy for paper to burn.
Four ways to speed up a reaction

Higher concentration (or pressure for gases): more collisions per second. Higher temperature: more particles exceed the activation energy. A rough rule: the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise. Greater surface area: powdered solids react faster than lumps. Flour dust can explode. Catalyst: see below.
Catalysts

A catalyst gives the reaction an easier path with lower activation energy and is not used up. It does not change the final products or amount. Iron in the Haber process. Vanadium pentoxide in making sulphuric acid. Platinum, palladium and rhodium in car catalytic converters, which convert CO and NOx into CO2 and N2. Enzymes: biological catalysts, e.g. amylase in saliva.
Rate laws and half-life

The rate is how fast concentration changes: rate = change in concentration / time. For a first-order reaction, the rate is proportional to the concentration, and the time for the quantity to halve, the half-life , is constant. Radioactive decay follows this pattern, as do many drug breakdowns in the body.
Half-life

A reaction has half-life 10 minutes. Start with 80 g. After 30 minutes? 30 / 10 = 3 half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g . Rate: concentration falls from 0.50 mol/L to 0.20 mol/L in 15 s. Average rate = 0.30 / 15 = 0.02 mol/L per second .
Not what you think

Catalysts are not consumed and do not shift the equilibrium. Exothermic does not mean fast. Activation energy decides speed. Heating speeds all reactions (it increases particles with enough energy), but enzymes stop working if overheated. Half-life is not half of the time to complete ; it never fully reaches zero in theory.
Cleaner exhaust: BS-VI

India moved to Bharat Stage VI emission norms nationwide in April 2020, leaping from BS-IV. Cleaner petrol and diesel plus better catalytic converters and particulate filters cut sulphur and tailpipe pollutants sharply. The converter is a catalyst: tiny platinum-group metal particles on a honeycomb speed up the conversion of CO and NOx into harmless gases.
Key takeaways

Reactions need collisions with energy above the activation energy. Faster with higher concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts. Half-life: quantity halves each constant time period. Think about it 1. Why does a fridge keep milk fresh longer? 2. Why does a lump of sugar dissolve slower than powder?
Chemical Equilibrium
Reactions that go both ways

Many reactions do not run to completion. They reach a balance where products form and revert at the same rate. This equilibrium decides how much ammonia a plant makes, how your blood stays at the right pH and why fizzy drinks go flat when opened.
Dynamic balance

In a reversible reaction (written with a double arrow, ⇌) the forward and reverse reactions both occur. At equilibrium their rates are equal. Concentrations stay constant, but nothing has stopped: molecules keep reacting both ways, like a busy escalator with equal people going up and down. Example: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
The equilibrium constant

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the constant is Kc Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b) Brackets mean concentration in mol/L. For ammonia: Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3). Large K (much greater than 1): mostly products. Small K (much less than 1): mostly reactants. K depends only on temperature.
Le Chatelier's principle

Henri Le Chatelier, 1884 : if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts to partly undo the disturbance. Add reactant: shifts toward products. Remove product: shifts toward products. Raise pressure: shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules. Raise temperature: favours the endothermic direction. Catalyst: no shift, only reaches equilibrium faster.
The Haber process as a puzzle
N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, exothermic (about -92 kJ per mole of reaction). Fritz Haber proved the method in 1909 and Carl Bosch scaled it up industrially by 1913.
Equilibrium in everyday life

A fizzy drink holds CO2 in solution: CO2(g) ⇌ CO2(aq). Opening the bottle drops pressure, so CO2 escapes. Blood contains a CO2 / bicarbonate buffer system keeping pH near 7.4. Oceans absorb CO2 forming carbonic acid, the root of ocean acidification.
Calculating Kc

A + B ⇌ C. At equilibrium [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10, [C] = 0.40 mol/L. Kc = [C] / ([A][B]) = 0.40 / (0.20 x 0.10) = 20 . Products are favoured. Le Chatelier check: if more B is added, equilibrium shifts forward, giving more C until Kc returns to 20.
Pitfalls

Equal concentrations are not equilibrium. Equal rates are. Catalysts do not change K or the yield, only the speed. Equilibrium does not mean the reaction has stopped. Pure solids and liquids are left out of K.
India's fertiliser backbone

India's urea industry relies on ammonia made by high-pressure equilibrium chemistry. Cooperative giants like IFFCO (founded 1967) and many public-sector units run plants where engineers tune pressure, temperature and catalysts using exactly these principles to maximise yield and cut energy use. Shifting to green ammonia from renewable hydrogen is now a stated national goal.
Key takeaways

Equilibrium: forward rate equals reverse rate; concentrations constant. Kc = products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient; depends only on temperature. Le Chatelier: systems oppose a disturbance. Think about it 1. Why use a compromise temperature in the Haber process? 2. Why does warm soda go flat faster than cold soda?
Acids, Bases and pH
Sour, soapy and everything between
Lemon juice, vinegar, stomach juices, soap, toothpaste, rain: all are acids or bases. Acid-base chemistry controls digestion, soil fertility, cleaning, pool water, and the Taj Mahal's marble.
Three definitions

Arrhenius (1884-87): acids give H+ in water; bases give OH-. Brønsted-Lowry (1923): acids donate protons (H+); bases accept them. Lewis (1923): acids accept electron pairs; bases donate them. Example: HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl-. HCl donates a proton, so it is an acid; water accepts it, so it acts as a base.
Strong and weak

A strong acid ionises almost fully: HCl, H2SO4, HNO3. A weak acid ionises only partly and sets up an equilibrium: acetic acid (vinegar), citric acid, carbonic acid. Strong bases: NaOH, KOH. Weak base: ammonia (NH3). Strength is not concentration. A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid can both be possible.
The pH scale
Søren Sørensen, 1909. pH = -log10 [H+]. Each unit is a tenfold change. pH 3 has 10 times more H+ than pH 4. Human blood is held tightly at about 7.4. Stomach acid is around pH 1.5 to 3.5.
Neutralisation and salts

Acid + base → salt + water. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. Antacids such as magnesium hydroxide neutralise excess stomach acid. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (the fizz): 2HCl + CaCO3 → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Indicators show the pH: litmus (red in acid, blue in base), phenolphthalein (pink in base), universal indicator (rainbow).
Buffers

A buffer resists pH change. It contains a weak acid and its salt (conjugate base). Added acid is mopped up by the base; added base by the acid. Blood uses the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer. Without it, a little acidic food could be fatal.
pH calculations

[H+] = 1 x 10^-3 mol/L. pH = 3 . 0.01 M HCl (strong): [H+] = 0.01 = 10^-2, pH = 2 . Neutralisation: how many mL of 0.1 M NaOH neutralise 20 mL of 0.1 M HCl? 1:1 ratio, same concentration, so 20 mL . If NaOH were 0.2 M, you need 10 mL.
Careful

pH 7 is neutral only at 25 °C. pH is not linear. pH 2 is 10 times more acidic than pH 3 and 100 times more than pH 4. Strong does not mean concentrated. Neutralisation does not always give pH 7 (weak acid with strong base gives a basic salt solution).
Turmeric and the Taj

Turmeric is a natural indicator: yellow in acid, turning reddish in base, which is why soap-washed turmeric stains turn red. Acid rain from sulphur dioxide of nearby industry was found to yellow the Taj Mahal's marble (calcium carbonate). The Supreme Court's 1996 orders (M.C. Mehta case) led to the Taj Trapezium Zone and shifts to cleaner fuel.
Key takeaways

Brønsted-Lowry: acids donate H+, bases accept. pH = -log [H+]; each unit is 10x. Acid + base → salt + water; buffers resist pH change. Think about it 1. Why is a weak acid still dangerous at high concentration? 2. Why do plants prefer soil of a certain pH?
Redox and Electrochemistry: Batteries
Electrons on the move

Rust, a burning candle, your phone battery and the aluminium in a foil roll are all redox chemistry: electrons transferred from one species to another. Harness that flow and you have a battery. Force it backwards with electricity and you can extract metals.
Oxidation and reduction

OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain. Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu. Zinc loses 2 electrons (oxidised), copper ions gain them (reduced). The zinc is the reducing agent ; Cu2+ is the oxidising agent . The two halves always occur together. Oxidation numbers track the shift. In Zn, it goes 0 to +2; in Cu2+ it goes +2 to 0.
Half-reactions
We split each redox reaction in two. Oxidation: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- Reduction: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu Add them so electrons cancel. This also helps balance difficult equations.
The galvanic cell

Alessandro Volta (1800) built the first battery (the voltaic pile). John Daniell (1836) made a steadier zinc-copper cell. Put each metal in a solution of its own ions, connect with a wire and a salt bridge . Anode = oxidation; cathode = reduction. Electrons flow from anode to cathode.
Cell voltage

Each half-cell has a standard potential. Zn2+/Zn is -0.76 V and Cu2+/Cu is +0.34 V. Cell voltage = E(cathode) - E(anode) = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V . More positive potential means a stronger tendency to be reduced. This ranks metals: reactive metals (Li, Na, Zn) sit at negative values.
Electrolysis and modern batteries

Electrolysis uses electricity to force a non-spontaneous reaction. Michael Faraday (1834) showed the amount of product is proportional to the charge passed. Uses: extracting aluminium (Hall-Héroult, 1886), electroplating, splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen. Lithium-ion batteries : Li+ ions shuttle between electrodes. The 2019 Chemistry Nobel went to Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino for them. Fuel cells combine H2 and O2 to make water and electricity.
Number of moles of electrons

Oxidation number of Mn in KMnO4: K is +1, four O is -8, so Mn = +7 . Faraday's idea: charge of 1 mole of electrons = 96,500 C. To deposit 1 mol of copper (Cu2+ needs 2 e-), you need 2 x 96,500 = 193,000 C . At 10 A, time = 193,000 / 10 = 19,300 s, about 5.4 hours.
Careful

Oxidation does not always involve oxygen. It is electron loss. Electrons do not travel through the salt bridge. Ions do, to keep the charge balanced. Rusting is redox. 4Fe + 3O2 + water → Fe2O3 (hydrated rust). Anode sign differs. It is negative in a galvanic cell and positive in electrolysis; it is always where oxidation occurs.
Delhi iron pillar and India's battery push

The Delhi iron pillar (about 1,600 years old, about 7 m tall) has barely rusted. Studies by metallurgists, including R. Balasubramaniam at IIT Kanpur, link this to its high phosphorus content, which helped form a thin, protective layer of iron hydrogen phosphate. That is redox chemistry in practice. India's 2021 PLI scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries aims for 50 GWh of domestic capacity.
Key takeaways

Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain. Galvanic cells turn chemical energy into electricity; E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode). Electrolysis forces reactions with electricity. Think about it 1. Why does a galvanised (zinc-coated) iron sheet resist rusting even when scratched? 2. Why can't you recharge most simple dry cells?
Metals, Alloys and Metallurgy
The Iron Age is still on

Bridges, cars, wires, coins, cookware, implants: metals underpin civilisation. Most metals sit in the ground as ores (compounds), and turning them into useful metal is metallurgy . Human history is even named after metals: Bronze Age, Iron Age.
Properties of metals

Metals are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (hammer into sheets) and ductile (draw into wires). The metallic bond, a sea of free electrons, explains all of this. Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature; sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife.
The reactivity series

From most to least reactive: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Ag, Au. Reactive metals (K, Na) react with cold water: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2. Middle metals react with acids. Gold and silver barely react, which is why gold is found native and is prized. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu.
Extraction methods follow reactivity
The ore is concentrated first. Then: Roasting heats sulphide ores in air; calcination heats carbonates in limited air; smelting reduces an oxide to metal.
Iron in the blast furnace

Haematite (Fe2O3), coke (carbon) and limestone go in the top; hot air goes in at the bottom. C + O2 → CO2, then CO2 + C → 2CO Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2 Limestone makes slag: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, then CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3, which floats and removes impurities. Aluminium is too reactive for carbon: Hall and Héroult (1886) electrolysed alumina dissolved in molten cryolite.
Alloys

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, so layers slide less: alloys are usually harder and stronger. Steel: iron with 0.2 to 2 percent carbon. Stainless steel: iron, chromium (about 10.5 percent or more), nickel. Brass: copper and zinc. Bronze: copper and tin. Solder: tin and lead (now often lead-free).
Iron from haematite

How much iron from 160 kg of Fe2O3? Molar mass Fe2O3 = 2 x 56 + 3 x 16 = 160 g/mol. So 160 kg = 1,000 mol. Equation gives 2 mol Fe per mole Fe2O3, so 2,000 mol Fe = 2,000 x 56 g = 112 kg . Which displaces which? Zinc and copper sulphate: zinc is higher in the series, so Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu works. Copper in zinc sulphate does not.
Careful

Reactive does not mean quick to decay. Aluminium forms a protective oxide film, which is why it lasts. Steel is not pure iron. Alloys are mixtures , not compounds, though they can contain compounds. Rust is not the same as all corrosion. Silver tarnishes by forming sulphide, copper turns green with a carbonate layer.
Delhi pillar, wootz and Zawar

The Delhi iron pillar : about 7 m tall, around 6 tonnes, made of nearly pure wrought iron (about 98 percent) in roughly the 4th to 5th century CE (associated with Gupta king Chandragupta II). It has stayed largely rust-free for about 1,600 years. Wootz steel from southern India, high in carbon, was exported and became legendary as Damascus steel. Zawar in Rajasthan is one of the world's earliest sites of zinc distillation. Tata Steel began producing at Jamshedpur in 1912 (company founded 1907).
Key takeaways

Extraction method depends on reactivity: carbon reduction for mid metals, electrolysis for reactive ones. Blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Alloys are stronger because mixed atoms block sliding layers. Think about it 1. Why can't aluminium be extracted by heating with carbon? 2. Why do we add carbon to iron to make steel, but not too much?
Non-metals: Hydrogen, Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen, Halogens
The elements of life and industry

You breathe oxygen, eat carbon compounds, grow food with nitrogen fertiliser, drink chlorinated water and may soon run vehicles on hydrogen. A handful of non-metals do much of the work of the living world and chemical industry.
What non-metals are like

Non-metals sit on the upper right of the periodic table. They are poor conductors (graphite is an exception), brittle when solid, and tend to gain electrons or share them. They form covalent compounds and acidic oxides (CO2 + H2O makes carbonic acid).
Hydrogen

The lightest, most abundant element in the universe. As H2 it is a colourless gas that burns to water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, with large energy per kilogram and no carbon dioxide. Made industrially by steam reforming of natural gas (CH4 + H2O → CO + 3H2) or by electrolysis of water. 'Green hydrogen' uses renewable power for electrolysis. Henry Cavendish identified it in 1766.
Carbon

Carbon appears in several forms (allotropes). Diamond: each C bonded to four others; hardest, insulator. Graphite: layers of hexagons, soft, conducts electricity. Graphene: a single layer of graphite. Fullerene C60: a football-shaped molecule (1985). Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the gas of respiration and combustion; carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous gas from incomplete burning that binds to haemoglobin.
Nitrogen and oxygen

Nitrogen makes up 78 percent of air. N2 has a triple bond, so it is very unreactive. Plants cannot use it directly; bacteria in legume roots, lightning and the Haber process turn it into ammonia and nitrates. Oxygen is 21 percent of air. Discovered independently by Scheele (about 1771) and Priestley (1774), named by Lavoisier. It supports combustion and respiration. Ozone, O3, in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV light.
The halogens

Group 17: fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I). They have 7 outer electrons and form X- ions or one bond. Reactivity decreases down the group: F2 is the most reactive. Appearance: F2 pale yellow gas, Cl2 green-yellow gas, Br2 red-brown liquid, I2 grey solid. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one: Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2. Chlorine disinfects water. Chlor-alkali industry: 2NaCl + 2H2O → 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2 .
Air and gases

How many litres of oxygen in 50 L of air? 21 percent of 50 = 10.5 L . Which displaces which? Add bromine water to potassium iodide: Br2 + 2KI → 2KBr + I2. Bromine is above iodine, so the solution turns brown/violet with iodine. Mass of hydrogen in 18 g of water: H is 2/18 of the mass, so 18 x 2/18 = 2 g .
Careful

Nitrogen is not what we breathe in for life. It is inert in the lungs. Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon , different only in arrangement. 'Chlorine in tap water' is a tiny dose that kills germs; chlorine gas itself is toxic. Hydrogen is not an energy source like oil; it is a carrier that must be made first.
Green hydrogen and iodised salt

India launched the National Green Hydrogen Mission in January 2023, with a target of 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen a year by 2030. Iodine (a halogen) prevents goitre. India's national goitre control efforts began in 1962, and universal salt iodisation became national policy by 1992. Tata Chemicals at Mithapur, Gujarat, produces soda ash and salt from sea brine.
Key takeaways

H2 burns to water; green hydrogen is made by electrolysis with renewable power. Carbon allotropes: diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerene. Air: 78 percent N2, 21 percent O2. Halogens grow less reactive down the group. Think about it 1. Why does graphite conduct while diamond does not? 2. Why is nitrogen gas so inert?
Transition Metals and Coordination Compounds
Colour, catalysts and blood

Ruby red, emerald green, blue copper sulphate, rust brown: transition metals give us colour. They also run catalysts that make fertiliser, carry oxygen in your blood (iron in haemoglobin) and power batteries and magnets.
What is a transition metal?
They occupy the d-block (Groups 3-12), such as Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn. Their atoms are filling d orbitals. They are typically hard, dense, high-melting and good conductors.
Four signature traits

Variable oxidation states: iron is Fe2+ or Fe3+; manganese goes from +2 to +7. Coloured compounds: d electrons absorb part of visible light; we see the rest. Catalysts: Fe in Haber, V2O5 in sulphuric acid, Ni in hydrogenation of oils, Pt in converters. Form complex ions.
Why colour appears

In a complex, ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels. An electron absorbs a specific colour of light to jump up. The compound shows the complementary colour. Copper(II) sulphate solution absorbs orange-red, so looks blue. Zn2+ and Sc3+ have empty or full d subshells, so no jumps, and their compounds are colourless.
Coordination compounds

Alfred Werner (1893) proposed that a central metal ion binds a fixed number of molecules or ions called ligands , through dative bonds (both electrons come from the ligand). He won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The number of ligand bonds is the coordination number . Six usually gives an octahedral shape; four gives tetrahedral or square planar.
Complexes in life and medicine

Haemoglobin: Fe2+ in a ring (haem) carries O2. Chlorophyll: Mg2+ complex, the green photosynthesis pigment. Vitamin B12: cobalt complex. Cisplatin: square-planar platinum complex, a cancer drug (approved 1978). EDTA: grips metal ions, used to treat lead poisoning and soften water.
Oxidation state of iron

In K4[Fe(CN)6], potassium is +1 (4 of them = +4) and each cyanide is -1 (6 = -6). Sum is zero: 4 + x - 6 = 0, so x = +2 . Fe is +2. Charge on [Cu(NH3)4]2+: ammonia is neutral, copper is +2, so the complex ion is 2+ . Coordination number = 4.
Careful

Zinc is not typically a transition metal as its d shell is full in all its compounds. A ligand does not need a charge. Water and ammonia are neutral ligands. Colour is not only from the metal. Changing ligands changes the colour. Catalysts are not magic. They offer an alternative reaction path through changing oxidation states.
Gems and colour

Ruby is aluminium oxide with a trace of chromium (Cr3+), giving a red colour; emerald (beryl) is coloured by chromium too, while blue sapphire owes its hue to iron and titanium. India's gem industry, with Jaipur for coloured stones and Surat for cutting and polishing diamonds, relies on such transition-metal chemistry to grade, treat and sell stones.
Key takeaways

Transition metals: variable oxidation states, colour, catalysis, complex ions. Werner (1893): metal centre plus ligands; coordination number often 6. Biology uses them: Fe in haemoglobin, Mg in chlorophyll, Co in B12. Think about it 1. Why is a solution of Zn2+ colourless while Cu2+ is blue? 2. How does a catalyst benefit from changing oxidation states?
Why Carbon Is Special: Hydrocarbons
Life is carbon

Over 90 percent of known compounds contain carbon. Your body, plastic, petrol, medicines, cotton, silk: all carbon-based. Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. Why one element makes so many compounds is the question here.
Carbon's superpowers

Four bonds: carbon has 4 outer electrons and shares them, forming four covalent bonds. Catenation: carbon atoms bond strongly to each other, forming long chains, branches and rings. Multiple bonds: single, double and triple. Isomers: same formula, different arrangement. Silicon is below carbon but its chains are weak, so life chose carbon.
A history note

Chemists once thought organic compounds needed a 'vital force' from living things. Friedrich Wöhler, 1828 , made urea from ammonium cyanate in a flask, a compound of living bodies, from inorganic materials. The vital-force idea faded. August Kekulé (1865) proposed the ring structure of benzene.
The hydrocarbon families

Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes (single bonds, CnH2n+2): methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10. Alkenes (one C=C, CnH2n): ethene C2H4, propene C3H6. Alkynes (one C≡C, CnH2n-2): ethyne (acetylene) C2H2. Aromatic: benzene C6H6, a stable ring. Alkanes are 'saturated'; alkenes and alkynes are 'unsaturated'.
Naming
The stem tells the chain length: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7, oct 8. The ending tells the family: -ane (single), -ene (double), -yne (triple).
Isomers

Butane C4H10 can be arranged as a straight chain (n-butane) or branched (isobutane, or methylpropane). Same formula, different properties. Isomers multiply fast: C10H22 has 75 isomers. This is another reason carbon chemistry is so rich.
Reactions of hydrocarbons

Combustion: complete: hydrocarbon + O2 → CO2 + H2O. Incomplete burning gives CO and soot. Substitution (alkanes): CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl in light. Addition (alkenes): C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2. Decolourising bromine water tests for double bonds. Hydrogenation: C2H4 + H2 → C2H6 with nickel catalyst.
Balance a combustion

Propane: C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O. 3 carbons: 3CO2. 8 hydrogens: 4H2O. Oxygen on right: 6 + 4 = 10 atoms, so 5O2. C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. Burning 44 g (1 mol) propane gives 3 mol CO2 = 132 g. A rule: formula of an alkane with 6 carbons is C6H14 (2 x 6 + 2 = 14).
Careful

Organic does not mean natural or healthy. It just means carbon-based; plastics are organic compounds. Not every carbon compound is organic: CO2, carbonates, and diamond are usually classed as inorganic. Isomers are not the same substance. Saturated does not mean 'full of water'. It means no double bonds.
Digboi, Jamnagar and E20

Digboi in Assam, where oil was struck in 1889 and the refinery began in 1901, is among the oldest operating refineries in the world. Reliance's Jamnagar complex in Gujarat is one of the largest refining sites on Earth. Ethanol, a carbon compound from sugarcane, now blends into petrol under India's E20 programme (20 percent ethanol, rolled out widely by 2025).
Key takeaways

Carbon forms four bonds, long chains, rings and multiple bonds. Alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2. Isomers share formula but differ in structure; combustion makes CO2 and water. Think about it 1. Why can carbon form millions of compounds while neon forms none? 2. How would you tell hexane from hexene using bromine water?
Functional Groups and Reactions
Small groups, big differences

Ethane is a gas; ethanol is in drinks and sanitiser; ethanoic acid is vinegar. Their carbon skeletons look similar. What changes is a small cluster of atoms called a functional group . Learn the groups and you can predict the chemistry of thousands of compounds.
What is a functional group?
A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic reactions. Molecules with the same group behave alike, whatever their size.
The main groups

Alcohol (-OH): ethanol C2H5OH. Aldehyde (-CHO): ethanal CH3CHO; formaldehyde. Ketone (C=O in the chain): propanone (acetone) CH3COCH3. Carboxylic acid (-COOH): ethanoic acid CH3COOH. Ester (-COO-): fruity smells; ethyl ethanoate. Amine (-NH2): methylamine; amino acids carry both -NH2 and -COOH. Halide (-Cl, -Br): chloroethane.
Four reaction types

Addition: a double bond opens: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH. Substitution: one atom or group replaced by another: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. Elimination: a small molecule leaves, making a double bond. Oxidation: alcohol becomes aldehyde or acid.
Ethanol: a case study

Making it: fermentation of sugars by yeast: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 . Industrial route: addition of steam to ethene. Oxidising it: ethanol → ethanal → ethanoic acid (vinegar), by oxidising agents or bacteria. Burning it: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O. Reacting with sodium: 2C2H5OH + 2Na → 2C2H5ONa + H2.
Esters and soap

Esterification: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, with a little sulphuric acid as catalyst. CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O Esters give fruit and flower fragrance. Reverse with a strong base (hydrolysis) and you get saponification : fat + NaOH → glycerol + soap. Soaps have a long non-polar tail that grips grease and a polar head that loves water.
Molar mass and identification

Ethanol, C2H6O: 2 x 12 + 6 x 1 + 16 = 46 g/mol . Fermenting 180 g glucose (180 g/mol) = 1 mol gives 2 mol ethanol = 92 g (theoretical). Which group? CH3CH2CH2COOH has -COOH: carboxylic acid, butanoic acid. CH3COCH3 has C=O between carbons: ketone.
Careful

Alcohols are not bases like NaOH; the -OH is not released as hydroxide. Carboxylic acids are weak acids , not strong. Fermentation is anaerobic ; vinegar-making needs oxygen. Industrial ethanol is made differently from drinking alcohol, though the compound is the same. Denatured alcohol is poisonous.
Sugarcane ethanol

India's sugarcane molasses ferment into ethanol, used in petrol blending, sanitiser (which saw huge demand in 2020), and chemicals. India's ethanol blending programme aimed at 20 percent blending (E20), cutting crude imports and emissions. Indian pharma also leans on organic synthesis: functional-group chemistry lies behind most generic drugs made in India.
Key takeaways

Functional groups: -OH, -CHO, C=O, -COOH, ester, -NH2. Reaction types: addition, substitution, elimination, oxidation. Fermentation: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2; esterification: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water. Think about it 1. Why do soaps clean grease but plain water cannot? 2. How do you turn ethanol into vinegar?
Polymers and Plastics
The material of the modern age
Your clothes, bottle, phone case, pipes, car tyres and even DNA are polymers: giant molecules made by joining thousands of small units ( monomers ). Plastics changed the world, and now trouble it.
Monomer to polymer

Like paper clips chained together, many small molecules link into a long chain. The repeating chain is written (-unit-)n, where n can be in thousands. Natural polymers: cellulose, starch, proteins, natural rubber, DNA. Synthetic ones: polythene, nylon, PVC, polyester.
Addition polymerisation

Monomers with a C=C double bond open up and join end to end. No by-product. n CH2=CH2 → (-CH2-CH2-)n polythene (polyethene). Other examples: PVC from vinyl chloride, polystyrene, Teflon (PTFE) from tetrafluoroethene, polypropene.
Condensation polymerisation

Monomers join and release a small molecule, usually water. Nylon-6,6: made by Wallace Carothers at DuPont (1935) from a diamine and a diacid, joined by amide links. Polyester (PET): diol + diacid, joined by ester links; the plastic of water bottles and fabrics. Bakelite (Leo Baekeland, 1907): first fully synthetic plastic, from phenol and formaldehyde.
Thermoplastic or thermoset

Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded: polythene, PVC, PET. Recyclable. Thermosets set permanently with cross-links: Bakelite, melamine, epoxy. They char rather than melt. Rubber: Charles Goodyear (1839) discovered vulcanisation, heating rubber with sulphur to form cross-links, making it strong and elastic.
The plastic problem

Most plastics are chemically stable, so they last hundreds of years. Millions of tonnes reach oceans; larger pieces break into microplastics that enter food chains. Solutions: reduce, reuse, recycle, redesign. Biodegradable plastics (like PLA from starch) break down, but often only in industrial composters.
Mass of a polymer chain

Ethene C2H4 has molar mass 2 x 12 + 4 = 28 g/mol. A polythene chain of 1,000 units has mass 1,000 x 28 = 28,000 g/mol . Addition: monomers in = polymer out, no loss: 56 g of ethene makes 56 g polythene. Condensation loses water: each amide link formed releases one H2O (18 g/mol).
Careful

Biodegradable does not mean it vanishes anywhere ; conditions matter. Recycling codes (1 to 7) identify type; the arrow symbol does not guarantee that it is recycled. Nylon is not natural silk. It was marketed as 'synthetic silk' in the 1930s. Plastic is not one substance but a huge family.
Single-use plastic and jute

India's Plastic Waste Management Rules (2016, amended since) set producer responsibility, and a ban on identified single-use plastic items took effect on 1 July 2022. India is a major producer of polyester and PET, with Reliance among large producers. Natural-fibre alternatives like jute , a cellulose polymer from Bengal, offer biodegradable bags.
Key takeaways

Polymers are long chains of repeating monomers. Addition: n CH2=CH2 → polythene. Condensation: loses water, e.g. nylon, PET. Thermoplastics remould; thermosets do not. Vulcanisation cross-links rubber. Think about it 1. Why is plastic's durability both a benefit and a problem? 2. Why can a thermoset not be melted and recycled like PET?
Biomolecules: Carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats, DNA
You are chemistry

Your body is built from four families of big molecules: carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids) and nucleic acids. Each is a polymer or an assembly of simple units. Understanding them explains food, energy, enzymes, inheritance and disease.
Carbohydrates: fuel and fibre

General formula roughly Cx(H2O)y. Glucose C6H12O6 is the body's main fuel. Sugars join into chains: Sucrose (table sugar): glucose + fructose. Starch: plants' energy store, long chains of glucose. Glycogen: the animal equivalent. Cellulose: plant cell walls, also glucose chains but joined differently; humans cannot digest it (fibre).
Proteins: the workers

Proteins are chains of amino acids (20 common ones), each with -NH2 and -COOH. Two amino acids join with loss of water to form a peptide bond . Shape decides function: enzymes, haemoglobin, antibodies, keratin in hair. Heat or acid denatures them: a boiled egg cannot go back. Frederick Sanger sequenced insulin in 1955 (Nobel 1958).
Fats and lipids

A fat (triglyceride) is one glycerol joined to three fatty acids through ester links. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C bonds (solid at room temperature, like ghee and butter). Unsaturated ones have C=C bonds (liquid, like most plant oils). Fats give about 9 kcal per gram, more than twice carbohydrate or protein (about 4). They also form cell membranes and carry vitamins A, D, E and K.
Enzymes and vitamins

Enzymes are protein catalysts. They fit substrates like a lock and key (or an induced fit), lower activation energy and work at body temperature and specific pH. Amylase breaks starch, pepsin breaks proteins in the acid of the stomach. Vitamins are small organic compounds needed in tiny amounts, e.g. vitamin C (scurvy) and D (rickets).
DNA: the information molecule

DNA is a polymer of nucleotides : sugar (deoxyribose) + phosphate + one of four bases, A, T, G, C. Watson and Crick, 1953 , building on X-ray work by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, proposed the double helix . The strands pair by hydrogen bonds: A with T , G with C . Three bases form a codon that specifies an amino acid. DNA is copied to RNA, then RNA is read to build proteins.
Base pairing and energy

One strand reads A-T-G-C. The partner strand is T-A-C-G . If DNA is 30 percent A, then T = 30 percent; G + C = 40 percent, so G = C = 20 percent each. Energy: 50 g of fat gives about 50 x 9 = 450 kcal; 50 g of sugar gives 50 x 4 = 200 kcal.
Careful

Fats are not all bad. You need essential fatty acids. Proteins are not only for muscle. Enzymes and hormones are proteins too. DNA does not make proteins directly ; RNA does the transfer. Cooked proteins are not destroyed nutritionally ; denaturing makes them easier to digest.
Khorana and the genetic code

Har Gobind Khorana , born in Raipur village (in present-day Pakistan) and educated in Punjab University in Lahore, shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for helping to decode the genetic code and later made the first synthetic gene. India's famed pulses, ghee and millets offer all the biomolecule groups: protein, fat and complex carbohydrate.
Key takeaways

Carbohydrates: glucose, starch, cellulose. Proteins: amino-acid chains joined by peptide bonds. Fats: glycerol plus three fatty acids, high in energy. DNA: double helix (1953), A-T and G-C pairing. Think about it 1. Why can we digest starch but not cellulose, although both are glucose polymers? 2. Why does a high fever risk damaging enzymes?
Chemistry of Everyday Life: Food, Medicine, Cleaning
Chemistry at home
Every kitchen, bathroom and medicine cabinet is a chemistry lab. Baking soda, soap, aspirin, preservatives and antiseptics all work by reactions you now know.
Cooking is chemistry

Baking powder and soda: sodium bicarbonate releases CO2 when heated or mixed with acid: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 . The gas makes cake and idli batter rise. Maillard browning: sugars and amino acids brown on heat, giving roast flavour. Fermentation: yeast or bacteria turn sugars into gas, alcohol or lactic acid (dahi, idli, bread).
Food preservation

Spoilage comes from microbes and oxidation. Preservation slows them: Salt and sugar pull water out of microbes (osmosis); pickles, jams. Acids (vinegar, lemon) lower pH. Antioxidants (vitamin C) stop fats going rancid. Cold and drying slow reactions. Food additives: colours, flavours, emulsifiers and preservatives (e.g. sodium benzoate).
How soap cleans

Soap is made by saponification : fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol. A soap molecule has a water-loving head and a grease-loving tail. The tails grip oil, the heads face water, forming micelles that wash away. Detergents are synthetic cleaners that work even in hard water, where soap forms scum with calcium and magnesium ions.
Medicines

Analgesics: aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, developed by Bayer, 1897) and paracetamol. Antibiotics: penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, developed as a drug by Florey and Chain around 1940. Antacids: neutralise stomach acid (magnesium hydroxide). Antiseptics on skin and disinfectants on surfaces. Antihistamines: reduce allergies. Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. Misuse breeds resistant bacteria.
Cosmetics and household chemistry

Toothpaste uses mild abrasives and fluoride, which strengthens enamel. Bleach (sodium hypochlorite) oxidises stains and kills germs. Never mix bleach with an acid or ammonia-based cleaner, as toxic chlorine or chloramine gas can form.
How much acid is in vinegar?

Vinegar is about 5 percent acetic acid by mass. In 200 g of vinegar: 200 x 0.05 = 10 g of acetic acid. Molar mass of CH3COOH = 60 g/mol, so moles = 10 / 60 = 0.167 mol . Baking soda: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. 168 g (2 mol, 84 g/mol each) gives 1 mol CO2 = 44 g.
Careful

'Chemical-free' does not exist. Water is a chemical. Natural does not mean safe (some mushrooms are deadly); synthetic does not mean harmful . Antibiotics do not treat colds (viruses). More soap does not mean cleaner; it is the micelle action that cleans.
Turmeric, generics and Hamied

Turmeric contains curcumin, a yellow antioxidant studied worldwide. India is often called the 'pharmacy of the world', a leading supplier of generic medicines by volume. Yusuf Hamied of Cipla offered triple-drug HIV therapy at about 350 US dollars per patient per year in 2001, opening access to millions. Hindustan Antibiotics in Pimpri began penicillin production in 1954.
Key takeaways

Baking soda releases CO2; fermentation makes bread, dahi and alcohol. Soap micelles trap grease; detergents work in hard water. Medicines like aspirin and penicillin are targeted organic molecules. Think about it 1. Why does salting preserve pickles? 2. Why mix soap with water, not oil, to wash oily hands?
Environmental Chemistry: Air, Water, Climate
Chemistry of the whole planet
Smog over Delhi in winter, the ozone hole, acid rain, polluted rivers, a warming climate: each is a chemistry problem, and each has a chemistry-led solution.
The atmosphere in layers

Troposphere (weather, up to about 10-15 km), stratosphere (ozone layer), then higher layers. Air is about 78 percent N2 and 21 percent O2. Pollutants alter the balance: CO, SO2, NOx, particulates (PM2.5 and PM10) and volatile organics.
The ozone layer

Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV-B light. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from fridges and sprays rise, UV splits off chlorine atoms, and each chlorine can destroy thousands of ozone molecules: Cl + O3 → ClO + O2. Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland warned in 1974; the ozone hole over Antarctica was reported in 1985. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs, among the most successful environmental treaties; ozone is recovering.
Greenhouse effect and climate

Gases such as CO2, CH4, N2O and water vapour absorb infrared heat radiated by Earth and re-emit it, keeping Earth about 33 °C warmer than it would be. Burning fossil fuels, C + O2 → CO2, adds more. CO2 rose from about 280 ppm before industry to above 420 ppm in the mid-2020s. Methane traps far more heat per molecule than CO2 over short periods.
Acid rain and smog

Burning coal releases SO2, vehicles release NOx. In air: SO2 → H2SO4 and NO2 → HNO3, so rain pH falls below about 5.6 (normal rain is slightly acidic from CO2). It damages marble, soil and lakes. Photochemical smog : sunlight, NOx and hydrocarbons make ozone and irritants at ground level. CO2 also dissolves in oceans : CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3, acidifying seas and harming corals.
Water chemistry

Hardness: dissolved Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand): oxygen microbes need to digest waste. High BOD means polluted water. Eutrophication: fertiliser nitrate and phosphate cause algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish. Toxic contaminants: arsenic, fluoride, lead, pesticides. Treatment: filtration, coagulation (alum), chlorination or UV disinfection.
Carbon to carbon dioxide

C + O2 → CO2. 12 g carbon gives 44 g CO2. So 1 kg carbon gives 44/12 = 3.67 kg CO2. Petrol (roughly C8H18): burning 1 litre releases about 2.3 kg of CO2, as most of the carbon in the fuel ends up as gas. A car using 5 L daily emits about 11.5 kg CO2 a day.
Careful

The ozone hole is not the cause of global warming. They are different problems, though some CFCs are also greenhouse gases. The greenhouse effect itself is natural and needed. The problem is enhancement. Clear water is not necessarily safe (arsenic is invisible). Acid rain is not melting people; it is mild but damaging over time.
Ganga, arsenic and clean air

India's Ganga Action Plan (1986) began sewage treatment to cut river pollution; Namami Gange followed in 2014. Groundwater arsenic affects the Gangetic plains in West Bengal and Bihar. The National Clean Air Programme (2019) targets reductions in PM2.5 and PM10 in polluted cities, and India has committed to net-zero emissions by 2070.
Key takeaways

CFCs destroy ozone; Montreal Protocol (1987) fixed it. CO2, CH4, N2O trap heat; CO2 above 420 ppm. SO2 and NOx make acid rain; fertiliser causes eutrophication. 1 kg carbon burns to 3.67 kg CO2. Think about it 1. Why was the Montreal Protocol more successful than most climate talks? 2. How can one chlorine atom destroy many ozone molecules?
Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity
When the nucleus changes

Ordinary chemistry rearranges electrons. Nuclear chemistry changes the nucleus itself, releasing millions of times more energy per atom. It powers stars, hospital scanners, nuclear plants and weapons, and it dates ancient bones.
Radioactivity

Henri Becquerel (1896) found uranium emitted rays; Marie and Pierre Curie discovered polonium and radium (1898) and named the phenomenon radioactivity. Unstable nuclei decay to become stable. The Curies and Becquerel shared the 1903 Physics Nobel, and Marie Curie won the 1911 Chemistry Nobel.
Three kinds of radiation

Alpha (α): a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons). Heavy, stopped by paper or skin. Dangerous if swallowed. Beta (β): a fast electron from a neutron changing to a proton. Stopped by thin aluminium. Gamma (γ): high-energy light. Needs thick lead or concrete. Alpha decay example: U-238 → Th-234 + He-4 . Mass numbers (238 = 234 + 4) and atomic numbers (92 = 90 + 2) both balance.
Half-life
The half-life is the time for half the radioactive atoms to decay. It is fixed for an isotope: iodine-131 about 8 days, carbon-14 about 5,730 years, uranium-238 about 4.5 billion years.
Fission and fusion

Fission: a heavy nucleus splits. Hahn and Strassmann found it in 1938; Meitner and Frisch explained it. U-235 + n → Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n + energy. The released neutrons trigger a chain reaction. Fusion: light nuclei merge, as hydrogen into helium in the Sun. Einstein's E = mc2 explains the energy: a little mass vanishes and becomes a lot of energy.
Uses and risks

Power: nuclear reactors give low-carbon electricity. Medicine: iodine-131 for thyroid, technetium-99m for scans, cobalt-60 for radiotherapy. Dating: carbon-14 for remains up to about 50,000 years old. Risks: radiation damages DNA; waste stays hazardous for long periods; accidents (Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011).
Using half-life

80 g of a radioisotope with half-life 3 days. After 9 days: 9/3 = 3 half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g . A bone has 25 percent of its original carbon-14. That is 2 half-lives, so age = 2 x 5,730 = 11,460 years . Balance: Radium-226 (Z = 88) alpha decays to radon (Z = ?): Z = 86, mass 222.
Careful

Radioactive does not mean glowing green. Reactors cannot explode like bombs. Fuel is far less enriched. Radiation is not always man-made. Bananas, granite and cosmic rays all give small doses. Half-life does not mean it is gone after two half-lives. 25 percent remains.
Bhabha's three-stage plan

Homi J. Bhabha founded the Atomic Energy Commission (1948) and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research. In 1954 he set out India's three-stage nuclear programme : (1) natural-uranium heavy-water reactors, (2) fast breeder reactors using plutonium, (3) thorium-based reactors, to use India's large thorium reserves in monazite sands. BARC, Trombay carries on the research; Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu is among India's biggest plants.
Key takeaways

Alpha, beta and gamma differ in mass, charge and penetration. Half-life is constant: halves each period. Fission splits, fusion joins nuclei; mass becomes energy (E = mc2). Think about it 1. Why is carbon-14 useless for dating a 100-million-year-old fossil? 2. Why is thorium attractive for India?
Green Chemistry and the Future of Materials
Making things without making a mess

Chemistry gave us medicines, fertiliser and plastics, but also pollution. Green chemistry asks a design question: can we make what we need while creating less waste and less hazard from the start? It prevents pollution rather than cleaning it later.
The 12 principles

Paul Anastas and John Warner (1998) listed 12 principles. Key ones: Prevent waste rather than treat it. Maximise atom economy . Use safer chemicals and solvents. Design for energy efficiency. Use renewable feedstocks and catalysts . Design products that degrade after use.
Atom economy

Atom economy = (mass of desired product / total mass of reactants) x 100. A reaction can have a high yield yet waste atoms in by-products. Addition reactions can reach 100 percent: C2H4 + H2 → C2H6 uses every atom.
E-factor and solvents

The E-factor (Roger Sheldon) is kg of waste per kg of product. Oil refining is under 0.1, bulk chemicals 1 to 5, and pharmaceuticals can be 25 to over 100. Greener solvents: water, supercritical CO2, ionic liquids, or no solvent at all. Catalysts cut energy and waste. Enzymes make drugs at room temperature in water.
Renewable energy and green hydrogen

Solar cells, wind, and batteries need new materials. Green hydrogen by electrolysis of water with renewable power, 2H2O → 2H2 + O2, offers a fuel and industrial feedstock without CO2. Green ammonia and green steel (reducing iron ore with hydrogen instead of coke) could cut industry's emissions.
Materials of tomorrow

Graphene: one-atom-thick carbon, strong and conducting; Geim and Novoselov isolated it in 2004 (Nobel 2010). Perovskite solar cells: cheap, efficient light absorbers. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs): sponge-like crystals to capture CO2 or water from air; the 2025 Chemistry Nobel recognised their development. Biodegradable plastics and recycling chemistry. Solid-state and sodium-ion batteries.
Atom economy

Making quicklime: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. Masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. Atom economy of CaO = 56 / 100 x 100 = 56 percent . E-factor: making 1 kg of drug creates 50 kg waste, so E-factor = 50 . Redesigning to 20 kg waste cuts it to 20. C2H4 + H2 → C2H6: 28 + 2 = 30 in, 30 out: atom economy 100 percent .
Careful

Green chemistry is not recycling alone. It starts at design. High yield does not mean low waste. 'Natural' solvents are not always greener if they need much energy to produce. Green hydrogen only counts as green if the electricity is renewable.
C.N.R. Rao and solar India

C.N.R. Rao is a leading Indian solid-state and materials chemist, known for work on oxides, nanomaterials and graphene. He received the Bharat Ratna in 2013. India co-founded the International Solar Alliance (2015) and has set big renewable targets, while the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) seeks green hydrogen and ammonia at scale. Indian industry and IITs work on greener catalysts and bio-based chemicals.
Key takeaways

Green chemistry prevents waste: 12 principles (Anastas and Warner, 1998). Atom economy = desired product mass / reactant mass x 100; E-factor = waste per product. Future materials: graphene, perovskites, MOFs, green hydrogen. Think about it 1. Why can a reaction with 95 percent yield still be wasteful? 2. What would you redesign in a product you use daily to make it greener?
